title: A business continuity tabletop: the river rises

injects.title: 05:30 Flood warning
injects.text: The river warning is raised to major. Water is expected in the headquarters basement, where the data center is, by about 08:00. 140 day staff are due in at 07:00; 12 night staff are on site.

injects.title: 07:30 Power
injects.text: Mains power is lost at headquarters. The data center runs on its generator, with fuel for about six hours.

injects.title: 10:00 Warm site
injects.text: The warm site reports it can start bringing systems up. IT asks which first.

injects.title: 13:00 Payments
injects.text: Orders are flowing at the warm site, but every card charge fails: the payment processor only accepts traffic from the headquarters address.

injects.title: Day 2, 09:00 Customers
injects.text: Hospital customers are calling about today's deliveries of surgical supplies. Some threaten to switch suppliers.

secondaryObjectives: Implement disaster recovery processes and test the plan with read-throughs, walkthroughs, simulations, parallel tests and full interruption tests
Prioritize business continuity requirements from a business impact analysis, including external dependencies

brief.situation: You coordinate business continuity at Pinecrest Medical Supply, a fictional distributor of surgical supplies to hospitals. Today the continuity team runs a tabletop exercise, and you play the coordinator. The facilitator reads a flood scenario in injects from 05:30: the river is rising toward headquarters, where the data center sits in the basement. Keep people safe, invoke the plan in time, recover in the order the business needs, and find where the plan fails.
handover: The business impact analysis gives order management and payments a maximum tolerable downtime of 24 hours, the warehouse system 48 hours, and email, file shares and payroll 7 days.
A warm site 200 km away holds replicas of the critical systems. This is an exercise: a decision made here is judged as if it were real.
howItWorks: The clock is the scenario's time. Each discussion takes scenario minutes; the facilitator's next inject arrives on the same clock and stops the wait.
The table shows each inject (one still waiting for the team's decision is marked), the roles, the communications and the decision log.
When the exercise ends you write the after-action report and explain your reasoning.

source.note: About six hours of generator fuel (the fictional site's figure).
The facilitator ends the scenario on day 2 at 13:00.

effects.log: The generator runs dry. The data center goes down hard, mid-transaction, with no failover started.
The facilitator ends the exercise. Time for the hot wash.

hotwash.question: For the after-action report: how the team protected people, when and why it invoked the plan, the recovery order it chose, and what the exercise showed about the plan.

parts.label: People and the declaration
parts.criteria: Puts people first at the warning (staff told not to come in, night shift accounted for); declares and fails over while the generator still runs, not after it fails.
parts.modelAnswer: Staff were told not to come in and the night shift was out by 06:00; we declared at 07:40 and failed over on generator power.

parts.label: Recovery by impact
parts.criteria: Recovers in the business impact analysis's order (orders and payments within their 24-hour tolerance first) and handles the external dependency through the supplier contract.
parts.modelAnswer: Orders and payments first, inside their 24-hour tolerance; the processor added the warm site's address under the contract.

parts.label: What the plan lacks
parts.criteria: Names the gaps (external dependencies missing from the impact analysis, an untested call tree, a warm site sized at 60 percent) and gives each an owner and a date.
parts.modelAnswer: Three gaps, each with an owner and a date: dependencies into the impact analysis, the call tree tested quarterly, and the warm site's capacity.

source.note: Each inject's decision within an hour of scenario time.
Every gap found has an owner and a date in the improvement plan.

noProgress.rationale: The exercise ended before the plan was invoked and before the generator ran out; nothing was tested, but nothing in the scenario was lost either.

unsafe.label: People put at risk
unsafe.narrative: In the scenario, 140 people drove toward a building the river was about to reach. No system is worth that.

hardDown.label: The data center went down hard
hardDown.narrative: The plan was never invoked while there was power to fail over cleanly; the generator ran dry with transactions in flight.

noReport.label: No after-action
noReport.narrative: The exercise found problems, and none of them will be fixed: there is no improvement plan.

exercised.label: The plan was tested and the gaps owned
exercised.when: documented and onTime >= 5 and rolesIn and gapsFound >= 3 and unowned <= unownedGaps and order == "bia"
exercised.narrative: People first, the plan invoked in time, recovery in the order the business needs, and each gap with an owner and a date.

partly.label: Partly tested
partly.narrative: The exercise ran, but decisions came late, the recovery order ignored the impact analysis, or a gap went unfound or unowned.

time_up.label: Time up
time_up.narrative: The run reached its time limit with no after-action report.

expertPath.text: People first: tell day staff not to come in and get the night shift out. Ask when the call tree was last tested.
Declare and fail over while the generator runs; brief the executives; ask how much load the warm site carries.
Recover in the impact analysis's order: orders and payments first. Ask which outside services each process depends on.
Have the supplier manager fix the processor under the contract; update hospital customers with a time for the next update.
Give each gap an owner and a date in the improvement plan.

exercised.headline: Good: the exercise did its job
exercised.body: People first, the plan invoked while it could still work, recovery by business impact, and the plan's gaps owned while they are cheap to fix.

partly.headline: Partly tested
partly.body: The criteria show what was missed: a late decision, a recovery order that ignored the impact analysis, or a gap found but not owned.

unsafe.headline: People come first
unsafe.body: Life safety comes before any system. Sending staff toward a flood is a decision no continuity plan allows.

hardDown.headline: Declared too late
hardDown.body: A warm site is only useful if you fail over while you still can. Waiting for the generator to fail turned a planned failover into a crash.

noReport.headline: Nothing will change
noReport.body: Without an improvement plan, the gaps the exercise found will still be there when the river really rises.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No after-action report was written before the run's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: People first: keep day staff away and get the night shift out. Declare and fail over while the generator still runs. Recover in the business impact analysis's order: orders and payments within their 24-hour tolerance, then the warehouse, then the rest. Fix the processor's allow-list through the supplier contract. Brief executives and update customers with a time for the next update. Use the exercise to find the plan's gaps: external dependencies, an untested call tree, a warm site at 60 percent. Give each an owner and a date.
